newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's new drug law comes under fire.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's new drug law comes under fire.

text.p: Cambodia's national assembly passed the country's first anti-drug law on Monday in a move analysts and human rights groups said would hurt ordinary citizens more than drug traffickers.
The anti-drug law provides for a minimum sentence of 10 years -- regardless of the quantity of illegal substance in question -- and a maximum of life imprisonment for possession or use of drugs.
"There are certain articles that don't protect the rights of the innocent," said parliamentarian Son Chhay, who was one of only three who voted against the law.
"Certain articles violate the constitution and human rights, and it could be used to punish the wrong people."
The only exception to the law is marijuana, which is sold openly and cheaply across Cambodia. The law provides for a minimum six-day sentence or maximum 30-day sentence for its possession or use.
The legislation will replace a section of the U.N. criminal code established by the U.N.'s Transitional Authority in Cambodia, which conducted the 1993 elections, experts said.

An international human rights observer called the law "a major disaster," and said parliament had been under significant pressure from the U.S. government and the United Nations. An official at the U.S. embassy declined to comment.
Earlier this year, Cambodia was included on the United States's list of major illicit drug producing and transit countries.
Minister of Information Ieng Mouly defended the law as an improvement over the initial version, although it might not succeed in stopping drug trafficking.

"The problem is smugglers. Cambodia is not a country that produces drugs but a transit place, where drugs can cross the borders. Cambodian officials need the means to stop that," he said. Cambodia borders Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.

The anti-drug law has been under fire from rights groups for its long jail sentences, phone tapping provisions, house and business searches and the seizure of assets -- all with what rights groups say are few limits on the power of authorities.

An earlier version was sent back for rewriting in June after an outcry from international rights workers, but they said the new version still does not contain sufficient provisions for the protection of human rights.

"The worst aspect is that the minimum prison term is 10 years in jail. Cambodia's drug law is unique in that it doesn't relate the severity of crime to the prison term. Whether someone deals 200 kilos or 200 grammes, they will both be thrown into deplorable prison conditions," said the rights observer.
